name: Chapter 11: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
description: Electron emission, photoelectric effect, Einstein’s equation, photons, de Broglie waves and NEET/JEE-style problems

cards.term: Cathode rays: what are they, and who confirmed it?
cards.definition: Streams of fast, negatively charged particles (electrons), seen in low-pressure gas discharge; J. J. Thomson confirmed it with crossed E and B fields

cards.term: What did Thomson measure for cathode-ray particles?
cards.definition: Their speed (0.1–0.2 c) and the specific charge e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg, independent of cathode material and gas: the particles are universal

cards.term: Thomson and the electron: when and what prize?
cards.definition: Named the particles electrons (1897); Nobel Prize in Physics 1906

cards.term: Millikan’s oil-drop experiment (1913): what did it show?
cards.definition: The charge on a drop is always an integral multiple of e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C: charge is quantised. With e/m, the electron mass follows

cards.term: Milestones near 1895–1897?
cards.definition: X-rays discovered by Röntgen (1895); electron by Thomson (1897)

cards.term: History note: NCERT credits Crookes with discovering cathode rays in 1870. Is that the whole story?
cards.definition: Cathode rays were observed earlier (Plücker, Hittorf 1850s–60s); Crookes studied them in the 1870s and suggested they are charged particles (1879). Exams ask Thomson → electron, Crookes → cathode-ray tube

cards.term: Why can’t free electrons simply leave a metal?
cards.definition: A departing electron leaves the surface positively charged, which pulls it back: it needs a minimum energy to escape

cards.term: Define work function φ₀. Unit?
cards.definition: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the metal surface; measured in eV (depends on the metal and its surface)

cards.term: Define electron volt.
cards.definition: The energy gained by an electron accelerated through 1 V: 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

cards.term: Three ways to supply the energy for electron emission?
cards.definition: Thermionic (heating), field (very strong E ~ 10⁸ V/m, as in a spark plug), photoelectric (light of suitable frequency)

cards.term: Photoelectrons: definition?
cards.definition: Electrons ejected from a metal surface by incident light of suitable frequency

cards.term: Teacher addition: typical work functions (eV)?
cards.definition: Cs 2.1, K 2.3, Na 2.3, Ca 2.9, Zn 4.3, Cu 4.7, Pt 5.6 (alkali metals have the smallest, so respond to visible light)

cards.term: Who discovered photoelectric emission and how?
cards.definition: Hertz (1887): sparks in the detector loop were enhanced when the emitter plate was lit by UV light

cards.term: Hallwachs’ observation with a zinc plate and an electroscope?
cards.definition: A negatively charged zinc plate lost its charge in UV; an uncharged one became positively charged: negative particles are emitted

cards.term: Lenard’s observation in an evacuated tube?
cards.definition: UV falling on emitter C causes a current to flow to collector A; it stops as soon as the UV stops (electrons attracted by the positive plate)

cards.term: Which metals respond to visible light and which only to UV?
cards.definition: Alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Cs, Rb) respond even to visible light; Zn, Cd, Mg need UV

cards.term: Threshold frequency: definition?
cards.definition: The minimum frequency of incident light below which no photoemission occurs, whatever the intensity; depends on the material

cards.term: Apparatus for studying photoelectric effect?
cards.definition: Evacuated quartz-window tube with emitter C and collector A; commutator to reverse the polarity; voltmeter and microammeter

cards.term: Why is the tube evacuated and fitted with a quartz window?
cards.definition: Vacuum: electrons reach A without collisions with gas molecules. Quartz: transmits UV (ordinary glass absorbs it)

cards.term: Effect of intensity on photocurrent (potential fixed, ν > ν₀)?
cards.definition: Photocurrent is directly proportional to intensity (number of photoelectrons per second ∝ intensity)

cards.term: Saturation current: definition and dependence?
cards.definition: The maximum current, when all emitted electrons reach A; ∝ intensity (for fixed ν)

cards.term: Stopping (cut-off) potential V₀?
cards.definition: The minimum negative (retarding) potential on A that reduces the photocurrent to zero

cards.term: Relation between stopping potential and maximum kinetic energy?
cards.definition: \( K_{max} = eV_0 = \tfrac12 mv_{max}^2 \)

cards.term: Effect of intensity on V₀ (same ν)?
cards.definition: None: V₀ is independent of intensity, so K_max is independent of intensity; curves for I₁ < I₂ < I₃ saturate at different heights but cut the axis at the same −V₀

cards.term: Effect of frequency on V₀, and on the saturation current?
cards.definition: V₀ increases with ν (V₀₃ > V₀₂ > V₀₁ for ν₃ > ν₂ > ν₁); for the same intensity the saturation current is the same

cards.term: V₀ vs ν graph: shape and meaning?
cards.definition: Straight line with slope h/e and intercept on the ν-axis = ν₀ (threshold). Different metals give parallel lines (same slope) with different ν₀

cards.term: Summarise the four experimental facts of photoemission.
cards.definition: (i) I_photo ∝ intensity (ν > ν₀). (ii) Saturation current ∝ intensity; V₀ independent of intensity. (iii) Threshold frequency exists; K_max rises linearly with ν. (iv) Instantaneous (~ 10⁻⁹ s or less)

cards.term: Time lag between light hitting the metal and emission?
cards.definition: Essentially none: about 10⁻⁹ s or less, even for very dim light

cards.term: Teacher addition: photocurrent vs applied voltage: what is the shape for V positive and negative?
cards.definition: Current rises with accelerating V until saturation; for negative V it falls to zero at −V₀. At V = 0 the current is non-zero (fast electrons still reach A)

cards.term: Exam trap: which quantities depend on intensity, and which on frequency?
cards.definition: Intensity → number of photoelectrons / saturation current. Frequency → K_max and stopping potential (and whether emission occurs at all)

cards.term: Wave-theory expectation for K_max with increasing intensity?
cards.definition: K_max should increase (larger E-field amplitude gives more energy per electron), contradicting observation

cards.term: Wave theory and the threshold frequency?
cards.definition: Predicts no threshold: a sufficiently intense beam over enough time should always free electrons

cards.term: Wave theory and the time lag?
cards.definition: Energy spreads over the wavefront, so an electron would need hours to gather φ₀; observed emission is instantaneous

cards.term: Which three observations does wave theory fail to explain?
cards.definition: Independence of K_max from intensity, existence of ν₀ and the instantaneous emission

cards.term: Einstein’s picture of radiation (1905)?
cards.definition: Radiation consists of discrete quanta of energy hν; an electron absorbs one quantum at a time

cards.term: Einstein’s photoelectric equation?
cards.definition: \( K_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0 \), i.e. \( eV_0 = h\nu - \phi_0 \) (more tightly bound electrons come out with less energy)

cards.term: Threshold frequency and wavelength in terms of φ₀?
cards.definition: \( \nu_0 = \dfrac{\phi_0}{h},\quad \lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\phi_0} \); λ₀ (nm) = 1240/φ₀(eV)

cards.term: Equation of V₀ versus ν?
cards.definition: \( V_0 = \dfrac{h}{e}\,(\nu - \nu_0) \): slope h/e (same for all metals)

cards.term: How does Einstein’s equation explain the intensity-independence of K_max?
cards.definition: One photon is absorbed by one electron; intensity only changes how many photons arrive (number of emitted electrons)

cards.term: How does it explain the threshold?
cards.definition: Need hν > φ₀ for K_max > 0: below ν₀ a single photon is too weak and electrons cannot pool energy from several photons

cards.term: How does it explain instantaneous emission?
cards.definition: Absorption of one photon by one electron is instantaneous regardless of the beam’s intensity

cards.term: Teacher addition: graph of K_max vs ν?
cards.definition: Straight line, slope h (Planck’s constant), x-intercept ν₀, y-intercept −φ₀; all metals give parallel lines

cards.term: Teacher addition: two metals with work functions φ₁ < φ₂ under the same light. Which gives more K_max?
cards.definition: Metal 1: K_max = hν − φ₁ is larger (V₀ larger, ν₀ smaller)

cards.term: Teacher addition: if the frequency is doubled, does K_max double?
cards.definition: No: K_max = hν − φ₀. It more than doubles: K₂ = 2hν − φ₀ = 2K₁ + φ₀

cards.term: Teacher addition: how is photocurrent related to intensity numerically?
cards.definition: If a fraction η of photons ejects an electron: \( i = \eta\,\dfrac{P}{h\nu}\,e \) (P = power of light)

cards.term: Millikan and Einstein’s equation (1906–1916)?
cards.definition: Millikan set out to disprove it but his slope of V₀ vs ν gave h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, confirming it (1916); Nobel Prize 1923 (also for e)

cards.term: Who got the Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect and when?
cards.definition: Einstein, 1921 (for the explanation of the photoelectric effect and contributions to theoretical physics)

cards.term: Photoelectric effect: frequency vs intensity
cards.definition: Below the threshold frequency no photoemission; above it each photon ejects one electron with Kmax = hν − φ0; intensity changes the photocurrent, not Kmax or stopping potential

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Photoelectric effect · picture

Light falls on a metal. Compare: (1) low-frequency light of any intensity, (2) high-frequency light, (3) the same high-frequency light with double the intensity.

Three cases, one after another.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Photoelectric effect · picture

Light falls on a metal. Compare: (1) low-frequency light of any intensity, (2) high-frequency light, (3) the same high-frequency light with double the intensity.

Below the threshold frequency ν₀ = φ₀/h no electron leaves, however bright the light: one photon has too little energy (hν < φ₀).

Above ν₀, each photon that is absorbed ejects one electron with Kmax = hν − φ₀. Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons, so the photocurrent doubles but Kmax and the stopping potential do not change.

cards.term: Energy and momentum of a photon?
cards.definition: \( E = h\nu = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda},\quad p = \dfrac{h\nu}{c} = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} \) (speed c, rest mass zero)

cards.term: Useful shortcuts: photon energy in eV and momentum?
cards.definition: E (eV) ≈ 1240 / λ (nm); p = E/c. e.g. 620 nm → 2 eV

cards.term: Photon picture: five key points?
cards.definition: (1) Light acts as particles in interactions. (2) E = hν, p = hν/c, speed c. (3) Energy independent of intensity (intensity = photons per second per area). (4) Photons are neutral (not deflected by E or B). (5) Energy and momentum conserved in collisions; photon number need not be

cards.term: Which experiment confirmed the particle nature of light (momentum)?
cards.definition: Compton scattering of X-rays by electrons (Compton, 1923–24; NCERT says 1924)

cards.term: Intensity in the photon picture?
cards.definition: \( I = \dfrac{N\,h\nu}{A\,t} \): number of photons crossing unit area per second × energy per photon

cards.term: Photons per second from a laser (Example 11.1)
cards.definition: E = 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; N = 5.0 × 10¹⁵ per second

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 11.1 · laser photons

Find the missing step.

Laser light of ν = 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz emits 2.0 mW. Find the photon energy and the photons emitted per second.
  1. E = hν = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 6.0 × 10¹⁴ = 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
  2. P = N E
  3. N = P/E = 2.0 × 10⁻³/3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 11.1 · laser photons

Find the missing step.

Laser light of ν = 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz emits 2.0 mW. Find the photon energy and the photons emitted per second.
  1. E = hν = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 6.0 × 10¹⁴ = 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
  2. P = N E
  3. N = P/E = 2.0 × 10⁻³/3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹
  4. N ≈ 5.0 × 10¹⁵ photons/s

cards.term: Threshold and stopping potential for caesium (Example 11.2)
cards.definition: ν₀ = 5.16 × 10¹⁴ Hz; λ ≈ 454 nm

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 11.2 · caesium

Find the missing step.

Work function of caesium = 2.14 eV. (a) Threshold frequency. (b) Wavelength of light whose stopping potential is 0.60 V.
  1. (a) ν₀ = φ₀/h = 2.14 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹/6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ = 5.16 × 10¹⁴ Hz
  2. ?
  3. eV₀ + φ₀ = 0.60 + 2.14 = 2.74 eV
  4. λ = 1240/2.74 nm ≈ 454 nm
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 11.2 · caesium

Find the missing step.

Work function of caesium = 2.14 eV. (a) Threshold frequency. (b) Wavelength of light whose stopping potential is 0.60 V.
  1. (a) ν₀ = φ₀/h = 2.14 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹/6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ = 5.16 × 10¹⁴ Hz
  2. (b) eV₀ = hc/λ − φ₀ → λ = hc/(eV₀ + φ₀)
  3. eV₀ + φ₀ = 0.60 + 2.14 = 2.74 eV
  4. λ = 1240/2.74 nm ≈ 454 nm

cards.term: Wave or particle: which description for what?
cards.definition: Interference, diffraction, polarisation: wave. Photoelectric and Compton effects (energy/momentum transfer): particle. Both matter, e.g. the eye’s lens (wave) and retina (photon)

cards.term: De Broglie’s hypothesis (1924)?
cards.definition:
Moving particles have waves associated with them: \( \lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv} \).
Reasoned from the symmetry of nature between matter and radiation

cards.term: Which quantity is the wave attribute and which the particle attribute in λ = h/p?
cards.definition: λ is the wave attribute; p is the particle attribute; Planck’s constant h links them

cards.term: Does the de Broglie relation hold for a photon?
cards.definition: Yes: p = hν/c gives λ = h/p = c/ν, the wavelength of the radiation (Exercise 11.11)

cards.term: Why don’t everyday objects show wave nature?
cards.definition: λ = h/mv is immeasurably small for large m: a 0.12 kg ball at 20 m/s has λ ≈ 2.8 × 10⁻³⁴ m

cards.term: Does the de Broglie wavelength depend on charge?
cards.definition: No: only on momentum (mass and speed)

cards.term: De Broglie wavelength in terms of kinetic energy?
cards.definition: \( \lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}} \)

cards.term: De Broglie wavelength of a charged particle accelerated through potential V?
cards.definition: \( \lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}} \)

cards.term: Teacher addition: electron accelerated through V volts. λ?
cards.definition: λ ≈ 12.27/√V Å (V in volts); proton ≈ 0.286/√V Å; α-particle ≈ 0.101/√V Å

cards.term: Teacher addition: same kinetic energy: electron, proton, α-particle. Order of λ?
cards.definition: λ ∝ 1/√m: λ_e > λ_p > λ_α. For the same accelerating voltage λ ∝ 1/√(mq): electron > proton > α

cards.term: Teacher addition: same de Broglie wavelength: photon energy vs electron kinetic energy?
cards.definition:
Same p: photon E = pc; electron K = p²/2m.
So \( \dfrac{E_\gamma}{K_e} = \dfrac{2mc}{p} = \dfrac{2c}{v} \) (photon much more energetic)

cards.term: Teacher addition: de Broglie wavelength of a gas molecule at temperature T?
cards.definition: \( \lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3mkT}} \) (using ½mv² = 3kT/2 for rms speed); for thermal neutrons, use \( \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mkT}} \)

cards.term: Teacher addition: Davisson–Germer experiment (beyond the rationalised NCERT text)?
cards.definition: Electrons of 54 eV scattered from a nickel crystal show a strong peak at a scattering angle of 50° (Bragg glancing angle 65°): λ = 2d sin θ ≈ 1.65 Å from Bragg’s law matches h/√(2meV), confirming electron diffraction

cards.term: Teacher addition: uses of matter waves?
cards.definition: Electron microscope (λ ≪ light, so higher resolving power), neutron and electron diffraction for crystal structure

cards.term: Points to ponder: what is physically meaningful for a matter wave?
cards.definition: Its wavelength and its group velocity (equals the particle’s speed); phase velocity has no physical meaning

cards.term: Wavelengths of an electron and a ball (Example 11.3)
cards.definition: Electron: 0.135 nm; ball: 1.47 × 10⁻³⁴ m

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 11.3 · electron and ball

Find the missing step.

de Broglie wavelength of (a) an electron at 5.4 × 10⁶ m/s, (b) a 150 g ball at 30 m/s.
  1. (a) p = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 5.4 × 10⁶ = 4.92 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m/s
  2. ?
  3. (b) p = 0.150 × 30 = 4.50 kg m/s
  4. λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/4.50 = 1.47 × 10⁻³⁴ m (unmeasurably small)
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 11.3 · electron and ball

Find the missing step.

de Broglie wavelength of (a) an electron at 5.4 × 10⁶ m/s, (b) a 150 g ball at 30 m/s.
  1. (a) p = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 5.4 × 10⁶ = 4.92 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m/s
  2. λ = h/p = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/4.92 × 10⁻²⁴ = 0.135 nm (X-ray size)
  3. (b) p = 0.150 × 30 = 4.50 kg m/s
  4. λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/4.50 = 1.47 × 10⁻³⁴ m (unmeasurably small)

cards.term: Are free electrons in a metal truly free?
cards.definition: Free inside the metal (constant potential, approximately) but not free to leave: they need extra energy to escape

cards.term: Do all conduction electrons need the same energy to escape?
cards.definition: No: they have an energy distribution (obeying Pauli’s principle). Work function is the least energy for the most loosely bound electron

cards.term: What does the photoelectric effect strictly show about light?
cards.definition: That energy is absorbed in discrete units hν in matter–light interaction; not quite the same as saying light is made of particles

cards.term: What is the crucial discriminator between wave and photon pictures?
cards.definition: The stopping potential: independent of intensity, dependent on frequency

cards.term: Chapter 11 quantities
cards.definition: Planck’s constant h: J s; [ML²T⁻¹]; E = hν; Stopping potential V₀: V; [ML²T⁻³A⁻¹]; eV₀ = K_max; Work function φ₀: J or eV; [ML²T⁻²]; K_max = E − φ₀; Threshold frequency ν₀: Hz; [T⁻¹]; ν₀ = φ₀/h; de Broglie wavelength λ: m; [L]; λ = h/p

cards.term: NEET pattern: light of wavelength λ ejects electrons with K_max. If λ is halved, K_max becomes?
cards.definition: K′ = 2hc/λ − φ₀ = 2K + φ₀ (more than doubled). If φ₀ = 0 it doubles

cards.term: NEET pattern: intensity of light is doubled at fixed ν > ν₀. Change in stopping potential and saturation current?
cards.definition: Stopping potential: unchanged. Saturation current: doubled

cards.term: JEE pattern: metal A and B have λ₀ in ratio 1 : 2 (A shorter). Same light on both: which has larger V₀?
cards.definition: φ₀ ∝ 1/λ₀, so A has the larger φ₀ and B gives the larger stopping potential (K = hc/λ − φ₀)

cards.term: JEE pattern: light of frequency ν gives stopping potential V₀; frequency 2ν gives 3V₀. Find ν₀ in terms of ν.
cards.definition: eV₀ = hν − φ₀ and 3eV₀ = 2hν − φ₀. Subtract: 2eV₀ = hν, so φ₀ = hν − hν/2 = hν/2: ν₀ = ν/2

cards.term: JEE pattern: given the V₀ vs ν graph, find h and φ₀.
cards.definition: Slope = h/e, so h = e × slope; intercept on the ν-axis = ν₀; φ₀ = hν₀ = e × |intercept on the V₀-axis|

cards.term: Board pattern: state three observations that wave theory cannot explain.
cards.definition: K_max independent of intensity; threshold frequency; instantaneous emission

cards.term: Board pattern: why does a photocell need a quartz window for zinc?
cards.definition: Zinc responds only to UV, which quartz transmits and glass absorbs

cards.term: Pattern: what is the momentum of a 6.63 × 10⁻²⁷ J photon?
cards.definition: p = E/c = 6.63 × 10⁻²⁷/3 × 10⁸ = 2.2 × 10⁻³⁵ kg m/s

cards.term: Pattern: relation between de Broglie wavelengths of two particles with masses m and 4m at the same kinetic energy?
cards.definition: λ ∝ 1/√m, so λ₁/λ₂ = 2 : 1

cards.term: Pattern: electron accelerated through 100 V. λ?
cards.definition: 12.27/√100 = 1.23 Å (about the spacing between atoms in a crystal)

cards.term: Pattern: effect of accelerating voltage doubling on the electron’s λ?
cards.definition: λ ∝ 1/√V, so λ falls by a factor √2 (to 0.707 of its value)

cards.term: Exercise 11.1: X-rays produced by 30 kV electrons: maximum frequency and minimum wavelength?
cards.definition: eV = hν_max → ν_max = 30 × 10³ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹/6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ = 7.24 × 10¹⁸ Hz; λ_min = c/ν_max = 0.041 nm

cards.term: Exercise 11.2: Cs (φ₀ = 2.14 eV) with light of 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz. K_max, V₀, v_max?
cards.definition: hν = 2.48 eV, so K_max = 0.34 eV (0.54 × 10⁻¹⁹ J); V₀ = 0.34 V; v = √(2K/m) ≈ 3.4 × 10⁵ m/s (key: 344 km/s)

cards.term: Exercise 11.3: cut-off voltage 1.5 V. K_max?
cards.definition: K_max = eV₀ = 1.5 eV = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

cards.term: Photon energy, momentum and rate (Exercise 11.4)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 11.4 · He–Ne laser

Find the missing step.

λ = 632.8 nm, power 9.42 mW. (a) Energy and momentum of a photon (b) photons per second (c) speed of a hydrogen atom with the same momentum.
  1. (a) E = hc/λ = 3.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (1.96 eV); p = h/λ = 1.05 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m/s
  2. (b) N = P/E = 9.42 × 10⁻³/3.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3 × 10¹⁶ per second
  3. (c) m_H = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 11.4 · He–Ne laser

Find the missing step.

λ = 632.8 nm, power 9.42 mW. (a) Energy and momentum of a photon (b) photons per second (c) speed of a hydrogen atom with the same momentum.
  1. (a) E = hc/λ = 3.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (1.96 eV); p = h/λ = 1.05 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m/s
  2. (b) N = P/E = 9.42 × 10⁻³/3.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3 × 10¹⁶ per second
  3. (c) m_H = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg
  4. v = p/m_H = 0.63 m/s

cards.term: Exercise 11.5: slope of V₀ vs ν = 4.12 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s. h?
cards.definition: Slope = h/e → h = 4.12 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.59 × 10⁻³⁴ J s

cards.term: Exercise 11.6: ν₀ = 3.3 × 10¹⁴ Hz, ν = 8.2 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Cut-off voltage?
cards.definition: V₀ = h(ν − ν₀)/e = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 4.9 × 10¹⁴/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = ≈ 2.0 V

cards.term: Exercise 11.7: φ₀ = 4.2 eV, radiation of 330 nm. Photoemission?
cards.definition: E = 1240/330 = 3.76 eV < 4.2 eV (equivalently ν < ν₀): No emission

cards.term: Exercise 11.8: ν = 7.21 × 10¹⁴ Hz gives v_max = 6.0 × 10⁵ m/s. Threshold frequency?
cards.definition: hν₀ = hν − ½mv² = 4.78 × 10⁻¹⁹ − 1.64 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ J → ν₀ = 4.73 × 10¹⁴ Hz

cards.term: Exercise 11.9: 488 nm light, V₀ = 0.38 V. Work function?

Exercise 11.10: de Broglie wavelength of
(a) 0.040 kg bullet at 1 km/s
(b) 0.060 kg ball at 1 m/s
(c) 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ kg dust at 2.2 m/s?
cards.definition: (a) 1.7 × 10⁻³⁵ m (b) 1.1 × 10⁻³² m (c) p = 2.2 × 10⁻⁹, so λ = 3.0 × 10⁻²⁵ m. All immeasurably small

cards.term: Correction: NCERT’s key prints 3.0 × 10⁻²³ m for Exercise 11.10(c). Right?
cards.definition: Slip: 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(1.0 × 10⁻⁹ × 2.2) = 3.0 × 10⁻²⁵ m. (3.0 × 10⁻²³ m would need m = 10⁻¹¹ kg.) The conclusion is the same

cards.term: Exercise 11.11: show that the de Broglie wavelength of a photon equals the wavelength of the radiation.
cards.definition: λ = h/p, and p = hν/c for a photon, so λ = h/(hν/c) = c/ν = the wavelength of the em wave

cards.term: Chapter 11 formula sheet
cards.definition: Photon energy: E = hν = hc/λ = 1240/λ(nm) eV; Photon momentum: p = h/λ = E/c; Stopping potential: eV₀ = K_max; Einstein’s equation: K_max = hν − φ₀; Threshold frequency: ν₀ = φ₀/h; V₀ vs ν: V₀ = (h/e)(ν − ν₀); slope h/e; de Broglie: λ = h/p = h/mv; Through potential V: λ = h/√(2mqV); electron 12.27/√V Å
